children: Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN, Financials), the technology and retail giant behind Amazon Web Services, has spent years selling the idea that cloud infrastructure can keep businesses running when things go wrong.
The Middle East just delivered a much harder test.

More than six months after strikes damaged AWS facilities in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates, Amazon says it cannot restore access to some resources and data that were kept only in the affected locations.
In Bahrain, the damage stretched across multiple availability zones and went beyond what AWS said its regional systems were designed to withstand.
Customers have moved workloads elsewhere, using backups when they had them.

AWS is still working to replace damaged infrastructure in one UAE availability zone, but Bahrain is different. Amazon says it has exhausted its options for recovering data that was not moved or backed up elsewhere.
That makes this more than a temporary outage.

AWS competes partly on reliability, and companies increasingly depend on cloud infrastructure for critical operations. The incident shows that even systems built with multiple layers of redundancy can run into limits when physical infrastructure itself is badly damaged.
Amazon plans another Bahrain update early next year.

Investors should watch what comes with it. The bigger question is whether AWS changes how it builds and protects data centers in regions where physical security has suddenly become part of the cloud-computing equation.

title: Amazon Just Learned a Hard Lesson About the Cloud
